question.text: Under Prospect Theory developed by Kahneman and Tversky (1979), how does an investor typically behave when facing gains versus losses?

answer.text: Risk-seeking about gains (hold winners longer) and risk-averse about losses (sell losers quickly)
Risk-neutral about both gains and losses
Risk-averse about gains (sell winners early) and risk-seeking about losses (hold losers longer)
Equally emotional about gains and losses of the same magnitude

explanation.text: The Logic: Prospect Theory states that choices are evaluated relative to a reference point. Investors become risk-averse about gains (selling winners early to lock in profits) but risk-seeking about losses (holding losers longer hoping for recovery). The workbook also notes that monetary losses hurt more than equivalent gains bring pleasure. The Trap: "Equally emotional about gains and losses" contradicts the asymmetry at the core of Prospect Theory — losses are felt more painfully than equivalent gains feel pleasurable. The first option reverses the correct behaviour pattern. Note: Prospect Theory was proposed by Kahneman and Tversky (1979) and is one of the foundational deviations from Standard Finance discussed in the workbook's behavioural finance chapter.
